title: Big Tech Earnings Deliver Mixed Signals for Micron's AI Memory Boom
excerpt: Alphabet's record $44 billion in AI capital spending signals sustained memory chip demand, but Tesla's earnings miss and Google's custom chip ambitions add uncertainty for the $1 trillion chipmaker.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Alphabet's $44 billion capital spending signals strong demand for Micron's AI memory chips.
  • Tesla missed earnings expectations, raising concerns about its AI hardware buildout.
  • Micron's stock fell 20% recently, despite an 800% surge over the past year.
  • Analysts are bullish on Micron, with 36 of 40 recommending buy and a median price target of $1,492.

Three of the most closely watched earnings reports of the quarter landed Wednesday evening, and their implications for Micron Technology are anything but straightforward. Alphabet, Tesla, and IBM each delivered results that pull the memory chipmaker's investment thesis in different directions — but the net signal, for now, tilts positive.

Micron shares closed at $959.48 on Wednesday after reclaiming a $1 trillion market capitalization earlier in the week on a 12% rally. The stock remains down roughly 20% from its highs over the past month, even as it has soared approximately 800% over the past 12 months on insatiable demand for AI-related memory and storage.

Alphabet's AI Spending Spree Is Micron's Tailwind

Google parent Alphabet posted a blowout quarter, reporting earnings of $9.11 per share — crushing the $2.87 consensus estimate by 216%, according to Zacks. Revenue reached $119.80 billion, with Google Cloud demonstrating 82% growth and YouTube advertising topping $11 billion for the first time in a single quarter.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=ubzMyU6bcWA

But the number that matters most for Micron is $44 billion. That is what Alphabet spent on capital expenditures in Q2 alone — a figure so large it pushed the company into negative free cash flow of $5.8 billion for the first time. The spending is overwhelmingly directed at AI infrastructure: data centers packed with GPUs and, critically, the high-bandwidth memory chips that Micron manufactures.

"Micron's record fiscal Q3 financial results and even stronger outlook for Q4 reflect the strategic value of memory in the AI era."

— Sanjay Mehrotra, CEO, Micron Technology

Micron's own fiscal Q3 results, reported June 24, underscore how directly it benefits from this spending: data center revenue hit $11.52 billion, up 653% year-over-year, and total revenue reached $41.46 billion, a 345.8% gain. The company guided Q4 revenue to between $49 billion and $51 billion.

Tesla Misses, IBM Steady

Tesla delivered a less encouraging read-across. The electric-vehicle and AI company reported earnings of $0.33 per share, missing the $0.50 consensus estimate by a wide margin, according to Zacks. Revenue of $28.26 billion did beat expectations and rose 26% year-over-year, but shares fell 3% in after-hours trading. Tesla's growing AI ambitions — including its Dojo supercomputer and autonomous driving infrastructure — represent a potential memory demand driver, but the earnings miss signals that its AI hardware buildout remains capital-intensive and uneven.

IBM, meanwhile, met expectations with earnings of $2.93 per share on revenue of $17.2 billion, a slight beat. Software revenue grew 5%, driven by Red Hat's 11% gain. The company said it is "investing aggressively" in quantum computing. IBM shares rose 2% after hours, offering a modest positive signal for enterprise tech spending.

The Custom Chip Wildcard

Not all the signals from Big Tech are bullish for Micron. Barron's reported earlier this week that Google is developing a custom chip code-named "Frozen v2" that would hardwire elements of its AI models directly into silicon, reducing the need for data transfers and, consequently, for high-bandwidth memory. The chip is reportedly targeted for 2028 deployment.

This is the tension at the heart of Micron's investment case: the same companies driving memory demand through massive AI buildouts are simultaneously working on innovations that could eventually reduce their dependence on it. For now, the spending is winning.

What's Next for Micron

Analyst Sentiment on Micron
›36 out of 40 analysts recommend buying Micron stock.
›Median price target is $1,492, indicating 56% upside.
›Recent selloff viewed as overdone by analysts.
Source: Analyst Consensus

ASML, the Dutch lithography monopoly, added fuel to the bull case when it raised its full-year revenue guidance to between 43 billion and 45 billion euros on July 15, up from a prior range of 36 billion to 40 billion euros. The company also plans to expand its EUV capacity by 30% in 2027. Wedbush analyst Matt Bryson called the expansion "consistent with the strong demand we are seeing for both leading-edge logic and DRAM to support AI builds."

Micron's next earnings report is expected September 22. With 36 of 40 analysts rating the stock a buy and a median price target of $1,492 — implying 56% upside — the Street's consensus is that the recent selloff is overdone. For Indian-American investors with significant exposure to the semiconductor sector, the coming weeks will test whether Big Tech's AI spending commitments translate into sustained returns for memory chipmakers or whether profit-taking and efficiency innovations cap the rally.
